strengths: The paper identifies a novel and practically relevant incentive issue in token-based LLM API pricing: providers can potentially report alternative tokenizations of the same output string and increase charges without changing user-visible text. This is an original angle connecting tokenization, economics, and LLM service design.

The formal principal-agent framing is clear and useful. The distinction between unverifiable tokenization, transparent generation traces, and incentive-compatible pricing gives the paper a coherent structure.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism is simple, interpretable, and directly addresses the specific tokenization-misreporting incentive when the output string is fixed. The characterization of additive pricing mechanisms by character counts is a useful conceptual result under that intended restriction.

The empirical proof-of-concept is concrete: experiments on LMSYS prompts and multiple open-weight model families show that plausible longer tokenizations can be found, especially at higher temperature/top-p settings. The paper also includes appendices with hardware, dataset filtering, model choices, and additional results.

The limitations and broader-impact discussion are unusually relevant: the authors acknowledge restricted pricing models, limited evaluation on open models, non-representativeness of LMSYS prompts, and dual-use concerns around the heuristic attack.
weaknesses: There is a material formal inconsistency in the incentive-compatibility definition. Definition 4 quantifies over any reported token sequence, not only sequences with the same string as the generated output. Under that definition, pay-per-character is not incentive-compatible because a provider could report a different, longer string. Theorem 6 and the main mechanism-design claim are only valid for the restricted same-string/tokenization-misreporting setting, so the formal statement needs correction.

The NP-hardness result is worst-case and relies on highly artificial vocabularies and next-token distributions. It supports a computational-complexity claim in principle, but gives limited evidence about the difficulty of optimal plausible retokenization for real BPE tokenizers and real LLM distributions.

The empirical overcharging results are suggestive but somewhat narrower than the presentation implies. Large gains mainly occur for permissive settings such as high temperature and p=0.99; at p=0.95 or p=0.90 the gains shown in the main figure are much smaller. The paper should calibrate claims like 'significantly overcharge' to these common deployment settings.

The threat model assumes the provider may misreport tokenization but, in the transparent setting, honestly reveals next-token distributions or enough information for plausibility checks. Since the same unfaithful provider could also manipulate or selectively disclose probabilities, the auditability story is incomplete without cryptographic, trusted-execution, or third-party verification assumptions.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript gives models, dataset filtering, hardware, and broad generation details, but I did not see a code release, exact software versions, seeds, or implementation details sufficient to reproduce the heuristic and plausibility checks without substantial reimplementation.

The proposed pay-per-character pricing solves the specific tokenization-reporting incentive but shifts incentives in ways that are not deeply evaluated, e.g. toward verbosity/shortness tradeoffs, Unicode/normalization edge cases, multilingual fairness, and provider/user preferences over output length and quality.

Presentation is generally strong, but there are minor correctness and polish issues in the appendix, including duplicated model naming and apparently mismatched license footnotes. These do not affect the main idea but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and under-discussed incentive issue in token-based LLM pricing: if the billed tokenization is not externally verifiable, a provider may have an incentive to report a longer tokenization of the same string.

The principal-agent framing is clear, and the simple observation that pay-per-token rewards longer reported tokenizations is easy to understand and potentially useful as a starting point for further work.
The paper includes both formal analysis and empirical proof-of-concept experiments across several open-weight model families, and it discusses limitations and dual-use concerns explicitly.
weaknesses: The central incentive-compatibility formalism appears flawed as written. Definition 4 quantifies over any reported token sequence, not only alternative tokenizations with the same string. Under that definition, pay-per-character is not incentive-compatible, since a provider can report an arbitrary longer string for higher reward. The later proposition and theorem implicitly use a same-string restriction, so the main mechanism-design result is either misstated or false under the given definition.

The threat model is not convincingly established. Many providers expose public tokenizers or usage accounting that users can approximately or exactly recompute for output text, while the paper repeatedly claims users have no grounds to verify token counts. The paper does not carefully distinguish hidden proprietary tokenizers, hidden chat templates, visible output strings, reported token IDs, and billing metadata, which weakens the practical motivation.

The NP-hardness result has limited relevance to the real setting. It is a worst-case construction over artificial vocabularies and next-token distributions, yet the paper draws broad conclusions about transparent LLM providers being unable to optimize misreporting in polynomial time. This does not show hardness for actual BPE vocabularies, actual model distributions, or realistic audit protocols.

The empirical attack evidence is modest and selectively compelling. The large 3x overcharge comes from the implausible strategy of billing every character as a token. Under the proposed plausibility constraint, gains are often small, especially for p=0.95 or p=0.90, and the strongest results depend on high temperature and permissive p values. The claim of significant overcharging without raising suspicion is stronger than the evidence supports.

The heuristic algorithm is weakly justified. It relies on token-id ordering as a proxy for BPE merge structure, evaluates only one resulting sequence, and is not compared to obvious search baselines or alternative splitting strategies. Runtime and profitability are argued qualitatively rather than measured against actual inference/accounting costs.

The proposed pay-per-character solution is under-analyzed. It removes incentives to retokenize the same output string, but does not address incentives to produce longer strings, alter formatting, use verbose phrasing, or manipulate output quality. The paper presents it as a simple fix despite acknowledging that pricing should also incentivize quality and usefulness.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper lists models, dataset, prompt filtering, and confidence interval calculation, but I did not see code, exact seeds, full preprocessing details, or enough implementation detail to reproduce the plausibility checks and heuristic efficiently. Some license footnotes also appear inconsistent.

The paper’s presentation is generally readable, but several claims are overstated relative to the assumptions: in particular, claims about unverifiability, lack of suspicion, practical vulnerability, and incentive compatibility require narrower wording and stronger evidence.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and underexplored incentive problem in LLM-as-a-service pricing: because the user sees only the output string/tokenization reported by the provider, pay-per-token billing can reward strategically longer tokenizations without changing user-visible text.

The principal-agent framing is clear and useful, and the paper connects tokenization details to economic incentives in a way that feels original relative to prior work on tokenization quality or model-substitution auditing.

The main story is supported by several complementary pieces: a simple proof that pay-per-token rewards longer reported tokenizations, worst-case hardness results for finding the longest plausible tokenization under sampling constraints, a concrete heuristic attack, and an incentive-compatible pay-per-character alternative.

The empirical section is modest but informative: experiments cover several open-weight model families and tokenizers, use LMSYS prompts, report repeated generations and confidence intervals, and show that plausible overcharging can be nontrivial, especially at higher temperature and high top-p settings.

The manuscript is generally well written and well motivated. The limitations and broader-impact discussion are unusually direct, including discussion of proprietary-model gaps, LMSYS representativeness, the possibility of misuse, and the fact that regulatory or user pressure may be needed for adoption.
weaknesses: There is an important formal inconsistency in the incentive-compatibility definition. Definition 4 quantifies over any reported token sequence, but the later Proposition 5 and Theorem 6 only hold for tokenizations with the same string. Under the written definition, any nonconstant pricing rule, including pay-per-character, would fail because a provider could report a different string with a higher price. This is probably fixable by restricting deviations to string-preserving misreports, but as written it weakens the soundness of the central mechanism-design claim.

The hardness result is worst-case and relies on constructed vocabularies and next-token distributions. It establishes an interesting computational barrier, but the paper sometimes rhetorically leans toward practical implications that are stronger than what the theorem alone supports for real BPE vocabularies and actual LLM distributions.

The empirical evaluation is a proof of concept rather than a broad measurement of real-world risk. It uses only the first 400 filtered LMSYS prompts, open-weight models, fixed generation lengths, and selected decoding regimes; proprietary APIs and common production billing/auditing details are not evaluated.

The heuristic attack is evaluated mainly by percent overcharged tokens, but the practical economics are less developed. The paper does not quantify end-to-end provider profit after added forward passes, batching overhead, logging/auditing risk, latency costs, or expected gain under realistic user traffic and decoding defaults.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives hardware, model names, dataset filtering, generation parameters, and licenses, but I did not see a code-release statement or sufficiently detailed pseudocode for all implementation choices needed to exactly reproduce the experiments. There are also some presentation/metadata issues, such as an apparent duplicated Llama model name in Appendix A and potentially mismatched license footnotes.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism removes this specific tokenization-reporting incentive, but it may introduce other incentives that are only lightly discussed, such as changing verbosity, Unicode/normalization handling, whitespace policies, language-dependent character economics, or strategic output formatting. These downstream pricing-design issues matter for deployment.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and under-discussed incentive problem in LLM API pricing: because users typically observe only the rendered string and usage count, pay-per-token billing can reward providers for reporting longer tokenizations of the same output.
The principal-agent framing is clear and useful, and the basic observation that pay-per-token pricing is not invariant to equivalent tokenizations is compelling.
The paper combines formal analysis, an explicit heuristic attack, and empirical illustrations across several open-weight model families, tokenizers, top-p settings, and temperatures.
The proposed pay-per-character mechanism is simple and interpretable, and the characterization of additive pricing mechanisms invariant to tokenization is a potentially useful contribution.
The manuscript is generally well written, with a good related-work discussion and an unusually explicit limitations/broader-impact section, including discussion of misuse risk.
weaknesses: A central formal issue is that the definition of incentive compatibility quantifies over any reporting policy and any reported sequence, but the later propositions/theorem only make sense for policies that preserve the output string. Without explicitly restricting feasible reports to same-string retokenizations, no nontrivial positive additive pricing mechanism is incentive-compatible, since a provider could report an arbitrary longer or higher-priced string. This substantially weakens the stated Theorem 6 and related claims.

The proof of Theorem 6 as presented appears incomplete for the stated iff claim: the appendix shows the necessary characterization using Proposition 5, but does not clearly prove the converse under the formal utility model. The converse also depends on the missing same-string restriction and nonnegative reporting costs.

The NP-hardness result is a worst-case construction over artificial vocabularies and next-token distributions. It does not strongly justify the practical claim that transparent providers cannot optimize misreporting for real LLMs, especially since the empirical heuristic is simple and effective. The paper should better separate worst-case hardness from practical difficulty.

The empirical evaluation is suggestive but narrow relative to the paper's policy claims: it uses small open-weight models, a small prompt sample, synthetic API conditions, and mostly high-temperature/top-p settings. The largest overcharging effects occur for p=0.99 and temperature above common default settings; effects are much smaller for p=0.90/0.95.

The profitability analysis relies on hardware- and implementation-specific energy measurements and a simplified cost model. Verification cost is treated as approximately constant per output, but plausibility checking of altered token sequences depends on sequence length, batching, model architecture, and serving stack; dollar costs, latency, and opportunity costs are not evaluated.

The threat model is under-specified. In practice, many providers expose token counts rather than token sequences, users may be able to retokenize outputs for public tokenizers, and opaque proprietary tokenizers create different audit assumptions. The paper would benefit from a sharper mapping between its reporting model and real API billing interfaces.

Reproducibility is weaker than expected: the manuscript contains a footnote saying the code is available, but the URL appears blank in the provided PDF. Experimental details are present, but the absence of code and exact preprocessing/scripts limits independent verification.

There are some presentation and consistency issues, including a duplicated/mistyped model name in the appendix, possible license footnote mismatch for Llama/Gemma, and several claims that are phrased more strongly than the evidence supports, such as 'without raising suspicion' based mainly on top-p plausibility.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and under-discussed incentive issue in token-based LLM pricing: billing depends on a representation that users may not directly observe. The connection between tokenization non-uniqueness, moral hazard, and pricing mechanisms is potentially useful.
The formal model is cleanly stated, and the pay-per-character characterization is intuitive and largely persuasive under the paper's additive-pricing and string-preserving assumptions.

The manuscript includes a limitations section that honestly notes important caveats, including additive-pricing assumptions, lack of proprietary-model evaluation, LMSYS representativeness concerns, and the possibility that pay-per-character pricing still incentivizes verbosity.

The empirical section makes a reasonable proof-of-concept attempt using several open-weight model families, LMSYS prompts, multiple top-p/temperature settings, confidence intervals, and energy measurements.
weaknesses: The central threat model is not convincingly grounded in real LLM API billing. For many services, users can independently retokenize the returned string with a published tokenizer, and billing is often contractually tied to that tokenizer or to reported usage metadata rather than arbitrary sampled token IDs. If the provider is fully malicious enough to lie about token counts, it is unclear why alternative tokenization is the decisive vulnerability rather than simple misreporting. This weakens the significance of the main claim.

The NP-hardness result is a worst-case construction over artificial vocabularies and next-token distributions. It does not establish that optimizing plausible alternative tokenizations is hard for real BPE/SentencePiece tokenizers and real LLM distributions. The paper leans on this result rhetorically, but its practical relevance is limited.

The empirical attack gains are narrow and sometimes small: the headline 11.2% overcharge appears for Llama-3.2-1B at p=0.99 and temperature 1.3, while more common settings such as p=0.95 are much smaller. The paper does not show that these gains persist under realistic production decoding, billing, moderation, streaming, caching, or tokenizer-audit workflows.

The financial profitability analysis relies on simplified energy-only costs and questionable assumptions about verification cost. Appendix C measures outputs in a restricted 200-300 token range, yet the text states verification cost is approximately independent of sequence length; this is not sufficiently demonstrated for broader lengths or deployment settings. Hardware reporting is also inconsistent: Appendix A says experiments use A100 GPUs, while Figure 11/Table 1 say a single H100.

Reproducibility is inadequate as presented. The main text says the code is available at a blank/incomplete location. There are also several concrete documentation errors, including duplicated model naming in Appendix A and mismatched license footnotes, which reduce confidence in experimental care.

The proposed pay-per-character solution is only partly satisfying. It eliminates incentives for string-preserving retokenization under additive pricing, but leaves the major practical incentive to increase output verbosity, which the paper acknowledges but does not address. It may also create undesirable cross-language and compression-related pricing effects that are only briefly explored.

Presentation is generally readable, but some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially statements that users can be significantly overcharged without raising suspicion and that the algorithm's cost is lower than additional revenue. These depend on assumptions that are not validated in realistic API settings.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-discussed incentive problem in LLM-as-a-service pricing: when users are charged per output token but cannot observe the actual generated token sequence, providers may be able to overcharge by reporting an alternative tokenization of the same visible string. This is timely, practically relevant, and connects tokenization to mechanism design in a novel way.

The formal principal-agent framing is clean and useful. The paper clearly distinguishes the generated token sequence, the reported sequence, the string-level value to the user, provider revenue, generation cost, and reporting cost. This makes the incentive argument easy to follow and gives the work more substance than a purely empirical vulnerability demonstration.

The theoretical results are meaningful: the paper shows why pay-per-token is not incentive-compatible, characterizes additive incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms, and motivates pay-per-character pricing as a simple remedy. These results are intuitive after the fact but still valuable, since they clarify exactly where the incentive problem comes from.

The proof-of-concept attack is convincing enough to establish practical concern. Algorithm 2 is simple, model-agnostic, and evaluated on several open-weight models from Llama, Gemma, and Ministral families using LMSYS prompts. The experiments show nontrivial overcharging under plausible-token constraints, especially for higher top-p and temperature settings.

The paper includes a useful limitations and broader-impact discussion. It explicitly notes that pay-per-character does not prevent verbosity manipulation, that proprietary models are not evaluated, that auditing requires assumptions about available information, and that the attack algorithm could be misused.

Presentation is generally strong. The motivation, definitions, figures, and main conclusions are clear, and the appendices provide proofs, additional experiments across temperatures/models, examples of modified tokenizations, and energy-cost measurements.
weaknesses: The strongest practical claims depend on assumptions about provider and user observability that should be sharpened. In many deployed APIs, users may know the public tokenizer and can compute the canonical tokenization of the returned string, while billing semantics may or may not correspond to the actual sampled internal token sequence. The paper argues that tokenization is non-unique, but the real-world relevance depends on whether providers bill by generated internal tokens, canonical re-tokenization, or reported usage metadata. This distinction deserves a more precise treatment.

The NP-hardness result is technically interesting but somewhat worst-case and artificial. The construction defines highly tailored vocabularies and next-token plausibility sets, so it does not strongly establish that optimizing misreporting is hard for realistic BPE tokenizers and neural next-token distributions. The empirical heuristic partly compensates for this, but the theorem should be framed more modestly.

The incentive-compatible pricing characterization is limited to additive mechanisms and to misreporting tokenization while preserving the output string. This is a reasonable scope, but the paper’s language occasionally sounds broader than the result supports. Non-additive contracts, bundled subscriptions, quality-based pricing, minimum fees, and hybrid schemes are outside the characterization.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism solves the retokenization incentive but leaves important strategic behavior untouched, especially verbosity inflation, whitespace/unicode manipulation, and output formatting choices. The paper acknowledges verbosity, but the remedy may therefore be less complete in practice than the headline suggests.

The empirical evaluation is solid but still relatively narrow. It uses 600-prompt subsets from LMSYS and open-weight models, with most main claims illustrated at high temperature values. More analysis of production-like decoding settings, batching, latency/cost tradeoffs, real provider tokenizers, and lower-temperature assistant use cases would strengthen the external validity.

Reproducibility has some gaps. The manuscript says the experimental code is available but the URL appears blank in the extracted text, and some experimental details are inconsistent or confusing, e.g. the hardware setup says A100 while the energy-cost appendix reports H100 measurements. Full prompts, seeds, exact model revisions, and code release details should be made explicit.

There are small presentation and polish issues: a duplicated model name in Appendix A, apparent license footnote mismatches for Llama/Gemma, and a few places where the paper says results are 'significant' or 'without raising suspicion' when this depends on the chosen plausibility criterion and on users having access to next-token probabilities.
